steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
At a high level, a Transformer is a sequence‐to‐sequence model that replaces recurrence (RNNs) with a pure attention mechanism.  Conceptually it works like this:

1. Input Representation  
   • Tokens (words or subwords) are mapped to vectors (“embeddings”).  
   • Since there’s no RNN to track order, fixed or learned positional encodings are added to these embeddings so the model knows each token’s position.

2. Self-Attention (“What should each word pay attention to?”)  
   For a given layer, every token’s representation is transformed into three vectors—Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V)—via learned linear projections.  
   • Compute attention scores by taking the dot product of each Query with all Keys, then scale and normalize with softmax.  
   • Use those normalized scores to form a weighted sum of the Value vectors.  
   • The result is a new contextualized representation for each token, since it “attended” to all others in the sequence.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   Instead of one Q/K/V projection, the model learns several in parallel (“heads”), each with different parameters.  
   • Each head can focus on different types of relationships (e.g. local vs. long-range).  
   • The heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly projected again.

4. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)  
   After attention, each token’s vector goes through a small two-layer fully connected network (same network for every position).  
   • Usually: Linear → nonlinearity (e.g. ReLU) → Linear.

5. Residual Connections & Layer Normalization  
   Both the multi-head attention block and the FFN have “add & normalize” steps:  
   • Add the block’s input to its output (residual connection).  
   • Apply layer normalization.  
   This helps training stability and gradient flow.

6. Stacking Layers  
   • The encoder stacks N identical layers of (self-attention → FFN).  
   • The decoder stacks N layers too, but each decoder layer has an extra encoder–decoder attention block (so the decoder can attend to the encoder’s outputs).

7. Encoder–Decoder Attention (in the Decoder)  
   • The decoder’s self-attention is masked so it can’t “see the future” (enforces auto-regressive generation).  
   • Then it attends to the encoder’s final representations (queries come from the decoder; keys/values from the encoder).

8. Final Prediction  
   • In tasks like translation, the decoder produces one token at a time.  
   • Each new token is fed back in (with updated positional info) until an end‐of‐sequence token is generated.  
   • A final linear+softmax maps the decoder’s output vectors to token probabilities.

Key Advantages  
   • Parallelizable across sequence positions (no step-by-step recurrence).  
   • Flexible attention lets it model long-range dependencies easily.  
   • Multi-head attention captures diverse relationships.

That’s the bird’s-eye view: positionalized inputs → layers of self- and cross-attention + feed-forward blocks, all tied together with residuals and normalization, yielding powerful sequence models like BERT, GPT and many others.
